title: Fresnel Clearance Percentage Calculator
description: Check obstacle clearance against the Fresnel zone with the Fresnel Clearance Percentage Calculator — measured against the 60% planning target. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 10 km link at 2.4 GHz whose path keeps 12.0 m clear of its 17.67 m first Fresnel radius is 67.9% clear — passing the classic 60% planning target with a little to spare.
quick_answer: The Fresnel Clearance Percentage Calculator compares the clearance your radio path actually has against the first Fresnel zone radius at the obstacle, and reports it as a percentage. Enter the clearance and zone radius and read the percentage — checked against the 60% working minimum.
steps_intro: Percent of the zone you keep clear is the link budget's quiet term:

body.t: A survey says the ridge clears the line of sight by so much — this page converts 'clears it' into the percentage engineers actually specify. The radius itself comes from the
Trees grow into zones. A path at 75% today with fast pines below is a 55% path in five years — the percentage makes the maintenance schedule arithmetic.
Installers sign off links against a clearance spec. Measuring the delivered percentage against the promised one is the acceptance conversation, in one number.
A link at 40% clearance often 'works' — until rain, growth or a new structure takes the rest. The percentage explains why marginal paths fail seasonally.

At the obstruction point the first Fresnel radius is 17.67 m (10 km, 2.4 GHz, midpoint). Clearance above the obstacle: 12.0 m → 12.0 ÷ 17.67 = 67.9% — comfortably above the 60% target, with the remainder as growth margin.

At exactly 0% (grazing the obstacle's edge) a link loses roughly 6 dB to diffraction in the classic knife-edge model — it works, wounded. Below the line of sight entirely, losses climb steeply. Percentages below 60 are borrowed performance.

popular_table.note: Clearance is measured at each obstruction point against the zone radius at that point (the zone is fattest at mid-path). Earth bulge and terrain heights enter the clearance figure itself — see the path-profile tools.

faq: Where do I get the radius at my obstacle?
From the Fresnel Zone Calculator with the obstacle's distances to each end — the radius swells toward mid-path, so position matters, not just the link's total length.

Above the highest obstruction (terrain, trees, structures) measured perpendicular to the direct line between antennas — the free space between the obstacle's top and the zone's lower boundary is the figure that counts.
Yes — it means the obstacle misses the zone entirely. Numbers above 100% are margins against growth and survey error, not waste.
Every significant obstruction gets its own percentage; the link inherits the worst one. A path is only as clear as its tightest point.
Rain does not change geometry — but wet foliage swells into the zone and refraction shifts under weather, which is why marginal percentages fail first in storms.
Raising either end lifts the line and fattens clearance everywhere; the percentage at the binding obstacle is how you size the raise before buying the mast.
It means the obstruction pokes through the line of sight itself by that share of the radius — the language stays consistent so bad news is still one number.
